query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial chemical substitution of Mo with additional Nb in the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy will reduce the problematic electronegativity difference and lattice distortion introduced by a high Mo content, thereby improving room‐temperature compressive plasticity while largely preserving its high strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, a disordered BCC solid solution exhibiting a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa but low plasticity due to the high Mo content.
generation.intervention: Reduce the Mo content and increase the Nb proportion—i.e., create a non‐equiatomic variant where a fraction of Mo is replaced by Nb while keeping Zr, Ti, and Hf unchanged.
generation.conditions: Alloys are prepared by arc melting (or similar processing) to ensure a homogeneous BCC solid solution. Room-temperature compressive tests are conducted under the same conditions as the baseline equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy to directly compare yield strength and fracture strain.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduced electronegativity difference and associated lattice distortions in the BCC matrix that facilitates easier dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Mo yields high strength via solid solution strengthening but also increases lattice strain and the electronegativity difference, which hinders dislocation mobility and reduces ductility. By partially substituting Mo with Nb—which contributes less to the problematic lattice distortion and has been associated with improved ductility—the alloy should retain much of its strength while permitting enhanced plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in room-temperature compressive plasticity (i.e., higher fracture strain) with only a minor reduction, if any, in compressive yield strength relative to the baseline 1719 MPa.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy that is strong (1719 MPa yield strength) but exhibits poor plasticity under room-temperature compression.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated only under modest Mo reduction; excessive removal of Mo may compromise the strength-enhancing solid solution effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise balance between the preserved strength and the improved ductility is uncertain and will depend on the exact fraction of Mo substituted. Experimental optimization is required to determine the ideal substitution level that maximizes ductility while maintaining high strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of NbZrTiHfMo-based alloys in which a controlled fraction (e.g., 20–40%) of Mo is replaced by Nb, keeping the other elements constant. Process all samples to attain a homogeneous single-phase BCC solid solution. Conduct room-temperature compression tests and record yield strength and fracture strain.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the partial substitution of Mo with Nb fails to produce a statistically significant improvement in compressive plasticity while maintaining a compressive yield strength close to (or not substantially below) the baseline of 1719 MPa, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.

The Table 3 and Table 4 summarize the results of compressive tests. Comparing the performance at room temperature, HfMoTaTiZr alloy has the best yield strength 1600 MPa; HfMoNbTaTi has the highest 27% fracture strain; comprehensively, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical properties (yield strength 1369 MPa and 27% fracture strain). The fracture strain increases from 4% for the HfMoTaTiZr alloy to 12% for HfMoNbTaTiZr. The presence of Ta can increase the yield strength but decrease the toughness. Ti seems to have no significant influence on strength, but it has a negative effect on toughness. Zr increases the strength; however, it strongly deteriorates the toughness at room temperature, because the fracture strain decreases from 27% for the HfMoNbTaTi alloy to 12% for HfMoNbTaTiZr. The presence of Mo, which has the highest shear modulus, increases the yield strength at room temperature from 929 MPa to 1512 MPa significantly. Nevertheless, the toughness decreases tremendously, fracture strain declines from > 50% to 12%.
